q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE way in which the Ottoman Empire expanded in the period c. 1450 to c. 1750.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason for Ottoman military success in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which the Ottoman Empire changed between 1750 and 1920.

sample_answers.a: The Ottomans conquered Constantinople (1453), then expanded across the Balkans, the Middle East, and North Africa under Selim I and Suleiman, building an empire on three continents.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, the Ottomans combined gunpowder weapons (artillery and muskets) with a meritocratic military system — the janissaries and a professional bureaucracy — that was more effective than the feudal levies of their Christian rivals.
sample_answers.c: From a conquering empire the Ottomans became a contracting one: they lost territory to Russia, Austria, and Balkan nationalists, accumulated foreign debt, and were reduced by 1920 to Anatolia before the Turkish Republic replaced the empire.

q1.stimulus:
Historians describe the Ottoman Empire as the most durable of the early modern Islamic gunpowder empires, lasting over six centuries. Its strength lay in a remarkable synthesis: Islamic legitimacy as caliphate, Roman imperial tradition inherited from Byzantium, and a meritocratic administration that recruited Christian boys through the devshirme, converted them to Islam, and trained them as janissaries and bureaucrats loyal only to the sultan. This system produced the conquests of Mehmed II and Suleiman the Magnificent. Yet the same empire that terrified Europe in 1529 was, by 1900, called the 'sick man of Europe' — outpaced by industrializing rivals, burdened by debt, and eroded by the nationalism it had once suppressed. The Ottoman story is thus one of spectacular rise and prolonged transformation.
—Historian's account of the Ottoman Empire in the period c. 1450–1750

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE feature of Ottoman government praised by Busbecq.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which the Ottoman system differed from European monarchies of the sixteenth century.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Busbecq, an Austrian diplomat, found the Ottoman system threatening.

sample_answers.a: Busbecq praises the Ottoman meritocracy: high offices, military commands, and judgeships are awarded for ability and service rather than birth, so talented men can rise from humble origins.
sample_answers.b: Unlike European monarchies where offices and titles were inherited by nobles regardless of competence, the Ottoman system (through the devshirme) recruited and promoted on merit, creating a more disciplined and effective administration and army.
sample_answers.c: As an envoy of the Habsburgs — the Ottomans' great rivals — Busbecq recognized that this efficient, merit-based system produced the formidable armies that had conquered Hungary and threatened Vienna itself.

q2.stimulus:
Among the Turks, honours and high posts are the rewards of great ability and good service. If a man be dishonest, or lazy, or careless, he remains at the bottom of the ladder, an object of contempt. This is why they are successful in their undertakings and why they are a menace to us. For we, with our birth and our ancestry, our inherited offices — what do we have to match their discipline and their merit? I tremble when I think of what the future must bring.
—Adapted from Ogier de Busbecq, Turkish Letters, 1550s

q3.directions: Use the map below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE pattern shown on the map of Ottoman territorial changes by 1920.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the Ottoman Empire's territorial losses in the nineteenth century.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which the map reflects continuity in the Turkish heartland despite imperial collapse.

sample_answers.a: The map shows the empire drastically reduced: the Balkans, North Africa, and the Arab provinces are gone, leaving only Anatolia and a small foothold in Europe — a fraction of the empire's sixteenth-century extent.
sample_answers.b: Balkan nationalist revolts (supported by Russia and other European powers), military defeats by industrialized rivals, and the empire's inability to match European economic and technological power stripped away its provinces.
sample_answers.c: Despite losing its vast empire, the Turkish core of Anatolia remained — the region from which the Ottomans had originally risen — and it became the foundation of the Turkish Republic established in 1923.

q3.stimulus: The map shows the territorial changes of the Ottoman Empire up to 1920, illustrating the empire's contraction from its sixteenth-century height — when it controlled the Balkans, the Middle East, and North Africa — to its remnant in Anatolia and eastern Thrace. The map visualizes three centuries of retreat: lost first to Austria and Russia, then to Balkan nationalists, then to Britain and France in the Middle East during World War I.
